quote: She criticises how I part my baby's hair, why she's wearing a singlet, how I've put her diaper on, how I'm holding her... you name it. I genuinely am not exaggerating when I say that around 95% of our video calls involve some form of criticism disguised as "helpful advice."
cx: First-time mother sending daily video calls to a mother-in-law who lives far away.

quote: On top of recovering from birth, my husband lost his job three months ago, we're under financial stress
cx: What else is weighing on her while the criticism continues.

quote: To top it all off, my wife is late in her third trimester with our second child. As it stands, the sleep prospects seem incredibly dim for both of us once the newborn arrives.
cx: Their 2.5-year-old accepts only her father at bedtime and night wakings.

quote: I *think* we might need to fix this before we have a newborn in the mix.
cx: Same father, weeks before the second baby.

quote: We are Norwegians, so yes, we have a very, *very* decent parental leave.
cx: Replying to a commenter about time at home after the birth.

quote: Recently we were told that fiancée is expecting to do the traditional postpartum confinement that is practiced in her country of origin, where the mother strictly stays in bed for 30 days and is not allowed to shower or eat cold foods (among many other requirements). They want someone to come stay for at least a month to take care of her and baby - cook and clean and everything else.
cx: An aunt-to-be; the mother-to-be has no family in the country.

quote: It doesn't sound like my brother plans to take any time off of work at all? […] I also don't have much leave, so I could at most do two weeks. […] My brother says "well we could pay someone to come help out but that would be expensive."
cx: Who is expected to cover the month after a December birth.

quote: If I had known they were planning to have a baby and what kind of help they were expecting I could have planned better, but... yeah, it is what it is. […] Also, I know nothing about caring for a baby...
cx: Same aunt-to-be on being the default helper.

quote: I keep seeing people say “everyone wants a village but no one wants to be a villager” in response to parents saying they are waiting to have visitors the first month or so after having a baby.
cx: A mother on the line used against parents who delay visitors.

quote: When I gave birth we let everyone come visit in the hospital but then wanted to have two weeks to ourselves after that and people were being so rude to us.
cx: Her own visitor plan after the birth and how family reacted.

quote: I didn’t want to spend the time I should be bonding with my baby cleaning before people come over and then small talking for hours. […] nobody helped with anything when they came over they just kept waking my baby up and made everything harder.
cx: What visitors were like in her first weeks.

quote: These are people who have only been in my life a few years. […] And also if it were a village they would actually help in raising him instead of using him for a photo op
cx: Why the 'village' line does not fit her family.

quote: The other thing that’s hit both my wife and me is the reality of having five children. […] Suddenly becoming hyper aware of the lack of time, the exhaustion, the fact we have very little family support. It suddenly feels overwhelming.
cx: A father of four boys, aged 9 to 10 months, expecting a fifth.

quote: At my wife’s mandatory request, we did all the “swaying” methods, timing, supplements, diet changes, you name it. I’m not a big believer in any of that stuff but I did it anyway for her.
cx: What they tried to conceive a daughter before this pregnancy.

quote: Its like everytime I go to pick her up im petrified im doing it wrong. Changing nappies is fine but most of the time my wife or MIL will jump in and take over.
cx: A first-time father with a baby nearly a week old, mother-in-law in the house.

quote: To mitigate this ive taken over everything else that isn't directly baby related. House is spotless. The fridge is full, bills are paid but still makes me feel like a shit dad when I watch how my wife and mil handle the bub in an incredibly proficient matter
cx: How he compensates for feeling useless with the baby.

quote: Why is there such a harsh response to anyone who expresses a desire to feel even a little covered if possible during labour? Why are people being shamed when they ask about delivery gowns or any kind of “modesty” measures that may be possible for labour and delivery?
cx: 30 weeks, first baby, single; on forum replies to women planning what to wear in labour.

quote: ideally I’d like to have someone at least say something to me before they just start doing anything invasive/embarrassing/humbling/involving removing clothes or something like that. Isn’t that sort of… a basic human right??
cx: What she hopes for from staff during labour.

quote: I didn’t even realize honestly that you can wear a bra/bralette during labour so I was sort of preparing myself for that part but now that I’ve seen people mention it I’m like… omg yes I will take anything over the no bra at all option if I’m allowed!!!!! Big ol win!
cx: Something she learned from replies that no one had told her.

quote: I’m terrified but when I hear stories about the really great nurses from people who have delivered at my local hospital it really does make a big difference.
cx: What eases her fear of labour.

quote: This is all so new and it feels like the time I’ve had to prepare went so fast, so I really am thankful for this comment and others like it. […] doing my best to cover all my bases but when did so many bases appear? There’s *so much* to learn for this wild ride.
cx: Thanking a commenter for practical, calm advice at 30 weeks.

quote: Several people have told me that I just have to submit to the process and accept a total loss of control and just sort of… deal with whatever happens in silence
cx: What people have told her about labour.
